text: During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was working on the roof of the storage tank when a rail that had been removed for maintenance fell and knocked the worker off balance, causing them to tumble onto the concrete below. The employee landed with a minor bruise and was able to get up after a quick first-aid check. The incident highlighted that the safety rail was missing at that section, and the maintenance team was notified to replace it immediately.

Night shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was walking across the unloading area and slipped on a wet patch left from a recent leak. The contractor caught himself and avoided a fall, but the spill was still present and could have caused a serious fall if the ground had been more uneven. The area was marked with caution signs, but the spill marker was missing, so the hazard wasn’t immediately obvious.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was working on the roof of the distillation column when the handrail that was supposed to support them gave way. The worker lost balance and fell about three feet onto the concrete floor, scraping his elbow and bruising his wrist. Luckily, the fall didn't hit any heavy equipment, and he was able to get up and report the broken rail, but the incident shows the handrail was either poorly maintained or not replaced after last inspection.

At Rig 4 on the night shift, a company employee noticed a faint orange glow near the valve chamber, indicating a potential gas leak. The worker quickly sealed the valve and called the fire alarm, but a damaged safety barrier failed to contain the odor. Thankfully, no ignition occurred, and the leak was contained before any fire started.

During the day shift at Terminal C a contractor was working on the valve pit when he failed to properly lock out the main isolation valve. He started the pump without checking the lockout tag, and the valve slipped open, sending a burst of high‑pressure gas toward the control room. The contractor and his team immediately shut down the pump, but the gas leak caused a brief flashover in the corridor, forcing an evacuation of the area.

On the day shift at Rig 4, a contractor was seen working on the rig floor without his hard hat and safety glasses. He was walking near the drill head when a loose piece of metal slipped from the rig and almost hit him. Luckily the contractor kept his feet in the safety shoes, but the lack of proper PPE could have caused serious injury.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was attempting to enter a maintenance hatch to replace a faulty sensor. He hadn’t secured the required air‑supplement system before entering, and a burst in the ventilation line caused a sudden drop in oxygen levels. The worker felt light‑headed, pulled back to the hatch, and the supervisor had to pull him out. The incident was logged as a near‑miss because the employee was not injured but the confined space entry protocol was not followed.

In the Pipeline Yard D on the day shift, a contractor was walking near the inspection gate when he forgot to wear his hard hat and steel-toe boots. He was only a few feet from a partially opened safety barrier that was still down. The missing PPE and lack of a visible barrier made it look like a near-miss, but the contractor could have easily slipped and fallen onto the unguarded pipe.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a company employee slipped while climbing a ladder to reach the top of the casing. He lost his footing on a wet rung, fell about 5 feet onto the concrete floor, and bruised his wrist. The fall was halted by the guardrail that was still in place, but the incident shows the ladder's footing was compromised by oil residue.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was checking the pressure relief valve when a sudden hissing sound indicated a possible gas leak. He stopped the work, sealed the valve with a clamp, and called the on‑site safety team. The leak was contained before any fire could start, but the contractor noted that the area’s fire extinguisher was missing and that the gas detector alarm had been disabled for maintenance.

Night shift at Pipeline Yard D: a contractor was using a hydraulic crane to lift a pipe segment when the boom tipped over sideways. The crane's safety latch was not engaged, so the load swung and struck the support rail, causing a small dent and a loud clang. Luckily nobody was hurt, but the incident shows the latch was missing and the crane’s stability margin was exceeded.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was working on the control panel for the main reactor isolation valves. The lockout tag on the energy isolation system was missing, so the valve was accidentally opened while the reactor was still under pressure. The employee only noticed the mistake when a pressure gauge began spiking, but the sudden pressure surge caused a minor leak that was quickly contained. The incident was logged as a near‑miss, but the lack of proper isolation equipment made the situation dangerous.

During the night shift at Rig 4, a company employee was walking along the service road when a delivery truck entered the area without stopping. The driver didn’t see the worker, and the vehicle clipped the employee’s side of a portable storage box, but the employee was only shaken and didn’t lose balance. The incident happened because the safety barrier that normally separates the road from the pedestrian path was missing that morning.

At Terminal C on the night shift a contractor was operating a hydraulic jack to lift a cracked valve. While the jack was on the load, the safety lockout bar had been removed to speed up the job and the jack slipped, throwing the valve against the concrete wall. The contractor was only grazed, but the incident shows the equipment hazard when a safety barrier was missing.

In the Maintenance Shop H during the day shift, a contractor was entering a ventilation duct that had been marked as a confined space. He forgot to put on a full-face respirator and when he reached the bottom, the duct’s access hatch blew open from a faulty latch, spilling a small amount of condensate onto the floor. The contractor slipped on the wet spot and fell, but he landed on a padded mat and only got a bruised elbow. The incident shows the hatch latch failed and the confined space entry was not properly guarded.

I was on the night shift at Refinery B and had to enter a vent pipe to check a leak. While inside, the air pressure suddenly dropped and the ventilation fan kicked off, so I nearly got stuck in the pipe. I managed to pull out safely, but there was no proper lock‑out/tag‑out on the vent line, and no oxygen sensor was installed. I flagged the missing barrier and the missing oxygen monitoring so it can be fixed before anyone else goes in.

At Rig 4 during the day shift, a contractor was working on the hydraulic system when the isolation valve failed to close. The valve remained open, and a sudden surge of pressure forced fluid into the pipework, causing a burst that sent high‑temperature fluid scalding the contractor’s sleeve. Luckily, the contractor only suffered second‑degree burns and was evacuated for treatment, but the incident showed that the isolation system was not functioning as it should.

At Pipeline Yard D on the day shift, a company employee was operating a hydraulic lift when the safety guard on the machine slipped off the frame and fell into the hydraulic cylinder. The guard was not secured, and the employee had to stop the lift immediately to avoid a serious injury. The incident highlighted a missing safety barrier that could have prevented the guard from falling.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a company employee was attempting to start the hydraulic pump after a routine maintenance check. The isolation lockout was not engaged, and when the operator turned the key, the system powered up unexpectedly. The employee was immediately pulled back to safety, but the sudden pressure surge caused a burst in the pipe, spraying hydraulic fluid across the work area. The incident highlighted a clear failure of the energy isolation procedure.

At Terminal C during the day shift, a company employee entered a maintenance hatch that had no proper lockout/tagout in place. He found the hatch unlocked, slipped inside, and immediately felt a sudden drop in oxygen levels. He had to exit quickly by climbing back out, but the hatch’s guard rail had snapped, so he almost slipped and cut his arm on the metal edge. No one was injured, but the incident shows how critical it is to secure all confined spaces before entry.

At Terminal C, during the night shift, a company employee was walking through the loading bay without wearing the required safety harness. The worker was near a high‑tension cable that had been temporarily lowered, so he nearly touched it and lost his balance. Fortunately, the fall was arrested by the guard rail, but it was a clear reminder that not wearing PPE can lead to serious injury.
An employee was driving a forklift when he struck a pallet of pipes. A pipe then hit his head, causing head trauma that required hospitalization.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a company employee slipped on a puddle of oil that had leaked from a damaged pipe. The employee was walking across the hatchway when the slick caused a loss of balance, but he managed to catch himself on a nearby support beam and avoided a fall. The spill was quickly contained with a spill kit, but the incident highlighted that the spill containment barrier on that section of the hatch was missing and needs to be installed ASAP.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a company employee was seen walking through the rig floor without a safety vest or hard hat. He was just about to step onto a wet area near the spill containment barrier when the barrier, which had been removed for maintenance, was not in place. He slipped a few inches, nearly falling onto the pipework, but the fall was stopped by a nearby safety rope. The incident was logged as a near‑miss because the employee was able to regain footing before any damage occurred.

At Terminal C during the day shift, a company employee was walking through the storage aisle and failed to wear his hard hat. He accidentally brushed against a stack of cracked piping, and the loose pipe slid onto the floor, causing a small spill. The employee slipped on the liquid but managed to get back up without injury. However, the missing helmet and the exposed pipe pose a serious risk to others.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee was seen walking past the hazardous spill area without wearing a protective glove. The employee’s bare hand brushed a sharp edge on the containment barrier, causing a small cut that bled and required immediate first aid. The lack of gloves was a clear PPE noncompliance issue that could have led to a serious injury if the employee had handled a larger spill.
While pulling a drilling pipe, the pipe broke and the jack fell onto the employee's foot crushing the steel toe portion into his foot.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee slipped while descending the steel ladder beside the tank stack because the handhold had a cracked plate. He almost fell to the ground but caught himself on the metal rung, so no injury occurred. The ladder should have been inspected before use.
An employee was cleaning a pin on a metal lathe when their hand got caught in the unguarded chuck of the lathe. The employee's left forearm, thumb, index and ring fingers were broken.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was operating a forklift to move barrels when the rear guard rail collapsed. The forklift’s rear bumper clipped the guard rail, sending the load slightly off balance. The contractor immediately stopped the machine and reported the incident; no one was injured, but the guard rail had to be repaired before resuming operations.

An employee was injured when another employee driving a pickup truck backed into him, pinning him between the truck and heavy equipment. He was hospitalized with a puncture laceration to the right buttocks.

On the day shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was stepping down from a 4‑meter high loading dock when the guard rail snapped, sending him to the concrete floor. He slipped and twisted his ankle, but no serious injury occurred; the incident was flagged as a near‑miss and the broken rail was replaced immediately.

While on the night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was entering a drainage trench that was marked as a confined space. The contractor didn’t secure the air monitoring device before entry and the hatch lock was left open. When the contractor reached the bottom, the hatch suddenly swung open, exposing them to a drop of liquid sludge. The contractor grabbed the edge and managed to avoid falling, but the incident shows the hatch lock failure and the lack of proper ventilation monitoring.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee was attempting to enter a storage tank that was supposed to be sealed. He slipped on a wet patch, nearly fell into the tank, but a quick grab from a co‑worker kept him upright. The tank was not properly depressurized before entry, so the employee had to retreat and report the missing pressure gauge.
An employee's left hand was caught in a print machine's rollers, amputating the index and middle fingertips.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking past the storage tanks when a sudden flare of flame popped up near the vent line. The worker realized a gas leak had started but it was just enough to ignite a small spark that fizzled out before it could spread. Luckily the safety valve was still functional and the flare was contained, but the employee had to evacuate the area and report the near-miss.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a company employee slipped off a ladder while moving a drill string to the rig floor. He lost footing on the rung and dropped onto the steel pipe supports below, scraping his shin but no serious injury. The fall happened because the ladder guard rail was not properly installed at the time.

While operating Rig 4 during the day shift, a company employee was cutting a pipe when a hydraulic cylinder unexpectedly released pressure. The sudden jolt threw the employee backward, causing him to hit his shoulder against the metal frame. Fortunately, he only suffered a minor bruise and the incident was reported immediately.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a company employee was checking the pressure gauges on the upstream gas line when a sudden sharp hiss of gas was noticed. The employee quickly moved back but the leak was already reaching the fire suppression system, which had been disabled for maintenance. The employee shut the main valve, stopping the flow, but a small spark from the valve handle ignited a faint flame, which was quickly snuffed out by the sprinkler system before it could spread. The incident was flagged as a near‑miss; the fire barrier was found to be partially obstructed by a storage container, which should be removed immediately.

Night shift at Drilling Unit F, a contractor was walking through the rig floor without his hard hat and safety vest. He nearly ran into the support beam of the drill rig because the safety barrier was missing, and his unprotected head would have hit the overhead pipe if he had not stopped in time. The incident was reported after the contractor realized he had violated the PPE requirements and the crew had to stop work until a replacement hat and vest were found.

An employee was taking a break by a baghouse after shoveling hot pellets that were being expelled from a cooler. While the pellets were still being expelled from the cooler hopper, a flame shot out of the discharge pipe, then backdrafted up the pipe into the cooler and then into the bag house. The employee suffered burns to the hands and arms from the resulting explosion.

At Pipeline Yard D on the day shift, an employee was walking the perimeter when a delivery truck ran a stop sign and nearly hit him. The driver lost control after braking late, but the employee was lucky to step aside in time. The incident shows the truck’s speed was higher than the yard’s posted limits and the employee’s alertness saved him from a collision.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a company employee was attempting to lock out the hydraulic pump when the isolation valve slipped open. The valve handle stayed in the “on” position and the hydraulic pressure began to rise, but the employee noticed the pressure gauge spiking and quickly shut the system off, preventing any actual damage. The incident highlighted a failure in the energy isolation procedure and a missing safety interlock on the valve.

On the night shift at Refinery B, a contractor was moving a set of piping from the storage area to the tank line when he slipped on a wet patch of oil that had leaked from a cracked pipe. He nearly fell over the edge of the concrete walkway and managed to grab a support rail just in time, but the spill had created a noticeable slip‑trip hazard for anyone walking past. The spill was cleaned up immediately, and a warning sign was posted while the contractor waited for a maintenance crew to seal the crack.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a contractor was entering a maintenance hatch that had not been properly sealed. He slipped on a wet patch and dropped a tool inside the hatch, creating a potential fire hazard. The hatch's safety lock was missing, so the contractor’s entry went unchecked and the area was not monitored until the tool was found.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee was cleaning the fuel transfer line when a sudden hiss of gas was noticed. The worker stopped and saw a small flame licking the pipe, but the flame was contained by the fire suppression system and the employee was able to evacuate the area quickly. The incident highlighted that the gas leak alarm was delayed, but luckily the barrier prevented a larger fire.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a company employee was walking across the site when a service truck accelerated out of control and almost ran over him. The driver was distracted, and the employee barely stepped aside in time. The incident was a clear near‑miss, highlighting a vehicle‑pedestrian interaction risk that needs to be addressed with better signage and driver training.

On August 4, 2025, an employee was fixing a jammed carousel and using a hook to manually adjust the carousel by hand. The hook slipped off and the employee fell to the concrete ground, resulting in hospitalization for a fractured right hip.

During the night shift in Pipeline Yard D, a company employee was working on the 12‑inch line when he noticed a faint odor of propane. He stopped the line and checked the pressure gauge, but the leak detector alarm didn’t sound because the sensor was still offline. The employee capped the pipe with a hand‑tied clamp, but the clamp loosened when he moved it, and the gas escaped, briefly lighting a spark from a nearby welding torch that almost ignited the spill. He quickly pulled the torch away, and a small puff of flame was contained before the fire broke out.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was operating a pallet jack to move a bulk container. While accelerating forward, the jack’s rear wheel struck the edge of a storage bin and spun off, causing the container to topple and roll onto the ground. The contractor narrowly avoided injury as the container landed on a soft soil patch, but the incident highlighted the lack of a proper guardrail around the bin area.

At Loading Bay G during the day shift, a company employee was unloading a tank when a gas vent opened slightly. The employee smelled a strong odor and saw a faint puff of flame, but the fire extinguisher was still within reach, so they quickly sprayed it and the flame died out. The gas detector alarm went off and the area was evacuated; no one was hurt, but the fire barrier around the vent was found to be missing and will be replaced.
An employee was throwing construction debris into a dumpster. A piece of block debris lacerated his right bicep. He was hospitalized.

Day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was going into the tank house for a routine inspection. The ladder had been propped up by a temporary bar, but it slid off when the worker moved, so the employee slipped and nearly fell into the tank. He stopped the entry, called for help, and the safety barrier was then put in place before anyone else entered.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a contractor was operating the pallet jack when the hydraulic cylinder failed to lock. The jack tipped over, sending a stack of empty drums onto the work floor. The contractor was only slightly shaken, but the incident shows the machine’s safety lock was missing and the barrier around the loading area had not been put up.

During the night shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee slipped on a patch of spilled drilling fluid that had not been cleaned up. The employee was just about to reach for a safety barrier that was still being erected when the slip occurred. The slip caused the worker to lose balance, but they managed to catch themselves on a nearby pipe and avoided falling. The incident highlighted the need for immediate cleanup and proper barrier installation before shift end.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was working on the flue gas stack when he was found without a hard hat and safety harness. He was standing near a hot vent and was about to touch a live pipe; fortunately, the guard rail was in place and prevented a fall. Still, the lack of PPE posed a serious risk, and the contractor had to be pulled away before any injury occurred.

During the day shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee was walking along the access road when a supply truck back‑saw him and had to brake sharply to avoid a collision. The truck’s emergency brake did not fully stop the vehicle, and the employee only narrowly dodged a minor impact. The incident highlighted that the pedestrian crossing sign was not visible in that spot, increasing the risk of future vehicle‑pedestrian interactions.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a contractor was working on a 12‑foot ladder to replace a faulty pipe valve when the ladder’s base slipped on a wet patch of concrete. He lost his footing, slipped, and fell about six inches onto the ground. Luckily he landed on a padded floor and only sustained a minor wrist sprain, but the incident highlighted the missing hand‑rail on that ladder set.

Day shift at Rig 4, a company employee was operating the drilling winch when the safety latch on the load‑hold arm failed to lock. The arm slipped slightly, causing a small hydraulic hose to come off and spill oil onto the floor. The employee immediately stopped the winch, flagged the area, and called for a repair crew to replace the latch and clean up the spill.
On March 16, 2019, an employee was using a knife to prepare a meal.  The knife slipped and cut the employee's thumb, amputating the end of it.

An employee stood up at their desk to plug a phone into their computer. When the employee went to sit back down, they missed the chair and fell, hitting their head. The employee required hospitalization for a post-concussive head injury.

Night shift on Rig 4, a contractor was welding in the rig bay when the spark hit a small leak of natural gas that was still on the vent pipe. The gas ignited a brief flare, but the fire alarm activated immediately and the fire suppression system kicked in, putting the blaze out before it could spread. The contractor was fine, but the incident revealed that the gas leak valve cover was missing, so we’re pulling the valve into a proper safety cage right away.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee attempted to enter the storage tank venting hatch to check a faulty pressure gauge. The employee didn’t use the required air‑monitoring and the hatch’s lock was missing, so the hatch opened unexpectedly, letting a sudden rush of toxic vapor into the space. The worker was able to exit quickly and pull the hatch closed, but the incident highlighted that the lock and proper confined‑space protocols were not in place.

At Loading Bay G on the day shift, a company employee was walking toward the loading dock when a forklift driver didn’t see him and the forklift brushed the worker’s shoulder, sending him stumbling back into a stack of pallets. The employee was shaken, bruised, but not seriously injured. The incident was called out as a near‑miss, and the driver was reminded to keep an eye on the pedestrian zone.

At Refinery B, on the night shift, a contractor was entering the 8‑foot tall venting stack through the access hatch. He had forgotten to secure the temporary entry seal, so as he lowered the harness the seal slipped and he slipped on the slick metal surface. He fell about 3 feet but was pulled up by a guard. The incident highlighted a missing safety barrier and the risk of a confined space entry failure.

At the maintenance shop H during the day shift, a company employee was working on the roof of the storage tank when he slipped on a wet patch left from a recent spill. He almost fell, but the guard rail held him in place. The spill area was not marked and the safety signage was missing, so the employee had to climb back down carefully.
An employee was cleaning debris from a machine when their left hand was caught in the in-going nip point. The employee sustained fractures and a crush injury to fingers of the left hand.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was working on a maintenance task when the hydraulic lift arm slipped out of the guard rail. He nearly got caught between the arm and the steel frame, but the guard rail caught his sleeve and he avoided serious injury. The incident highlights that the guard rail was not properly secured to the lift frame, creating a machinery hazard for anyone in the area.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a company employee slipped on a wet patch of oil that had leaked from a leaking pipe near the loading dock. The floor was not marked with any warning tape and the spill had spread beyond the containment barrier. The employee caught herself on a nearby metal post and was able to recover without injury, but the incident revealed that the spill containment barrier was missing in that area.

In Maintenance Shop H during the night shift, a company employee was working on a hydraulic press when the guard door failed to latch properly. The employee stepped back just in time, but the press moved unexpectedly, sending a metal arm into the workspace. Luckily, no one was hit, but the incident shows the guard was missing a lock.

An employee was removing an ambulance off a lift jack when the pressure against the jack caused the handle to kick upward, striking the employee on the left side of the head, neck, and jaw. The employee suffered injuries that required hospitalization.

During the day shift at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was walking across the loading dock when a discarded oil container fell into a shallow trench that had no guardrail. The contractor nearly slipped and caught himself on the edge, but the container rolled over and damaged a nearby pipe. The incident was a near‑miss but caused a small leak that required immediate containment.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was climbing a 12‑meter ladder to replace a burner vent. The ladder's guardrail was missing on the right side, so the contractor slipped but caught himself on the side rail, landing on his back but not hitting the platform. No injuries were reported, but the incident showed a clear lapse in safety equipment.

Night shift on Rig 4 when a company employee was trying to start the drilling motor without the isolation lock being engaged. The lockout tag was missing and the pressure release valve had not been closed. The employee almost got caught in the rotating part when the motor started, but a quick stop by the crew prevented injury.

At Terminal C on the day shift, a contractor was working on the roof of the storage bay when the guard rail that had been set up for his task collapsed. The rail was only partially secured, and as he leaned to check a pipe, he slipped and fell about 3 feet onto the concrete floor below. Luckily he only sustained a minor wrist sprain and was treated on site.

At Rig 4, during the day shift, a company employee was walking around the drill floor without wearing a hard hat or safety vest, despite the hard‑hat zone signs. The employee was nearly struck by a falling drill pipe that slipped from a nearby rigging rig. No one was injured, but the incident highlighted a clear PPE noncompliance that could have caused serious injury.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was handling a pressure line when a small spark ignited a flammable vapor that had leaked from a cracked valve. The flame spread quickly but was stopped by the automatic fire suppression system before it could reach the storage tanks. The employee had to evacuate the area and report the incident, but no one was injured.
notes: ignition source not specified as hot-work task; borderline

text: During the night shift at Refinery B, a company employee entered a vent hood to replace a worn gasket. The hatch was locked, but the latch failed, and the employee slipped and fell onto the piping, breaking a wrench and causing a small cut on his forearm. No fire or gas leak occurred, but the incident highlighted the need for a proper lockout-tagout procedure before any confined space entry.

At Loading Bay G on the day shift a company employee was unloading a tanker when a small fire sparked in the rigging gear. The employee noticed a gas odor and immediately shut off the valve, but the fire suppression barrier was missing, so the flame spread to the adjacent pallet of flammable drums. He managed to use the portable extinguisher before the flames grew, but the barrier failure meant the fire could have spread farther. The incident was reported to the supervisor and the barrier was installed immediately.
notes: fire event but no explicit hot-work task; borderline

text: During the night shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking through the chemical storage area without wearing the required hard hat and safety goggles. The worker walked right next to a leaking pipe; the exposed skin could have come into contact with the corrosive fluid, but the employee stopped just before the spray reached them. The incident was logged as a near‑miss because the PPE omission could have caused a serious burn if the leak had worsened.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a company employee was climbing the outer support ladder to replace a loose pipe. He lost his footing on a wet rung and slipped, falling about two meters to the concrete floor. He sustained minor bruises and a sprained wrist, but the fall did not hit any equipment or personnel.

During the night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was working on a section of the 40‑barline. While tightening the lockout tag on the isolation valve, the contractor noticed the lockout pin had not fully seated and the valve still had pressure behind it. The contractor immediately backed up and reported the failure, but the valve’s safety valve had already been partially released, sending a burst of hot steam toward the work zone. The incident was contained before any injury, but the missing lockout barrier highlighted a serious procedural lapse.
An employee was running a cable through trees when he came in contact with overhead powerlines, suffering second degree burns on his wrist.

On Rig 4 during the day shift, a company employee was climbing the rig ladder to replace a missing guard on the pipe‑handling platform. While reaching for a bolt, the guard had slid off, and the employee slipped, losing his footing for a split second before grabbing the nearest rail. He was able to recover without injury, but the incident shows the platform guard was either not installed or had failed, creating a fall hazard.
An employee was pushing a loaded molding cart through the store when they tripped and fell over the cart onto the floor, resulting in broken bones.

At Loading Bay G on the night shift, a company employee was handling a spill container without wearing the required gloves. He slipped on a wet spot and almost slipped into the spill, but the safety guard stopped him. The lack of PPE put him at risk and the incident was logged as a near‑miss.

Night shift at Rig 4 when a company employee was trying to lock out the hydraulic pump after the work was done, but the lock‑out tag didn’t engage properly. The pump slipped back on and the employee was forced to grab it at the last second, missing a serious kick‑back. The incident shows the energy isolation was not correctly secured.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a contractor was operating the drilling winch when the winch gearbox overheated and the safety latch on the load release lever slipped. The load swung across the rig floor, narrowly missing a nearby worker and coming to rest against the safety fence, which had been removed for maintenance. The contractor had to stop the machine, cool the gearbox, and re‑install the latch before resuming work.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a company employee was working on the drilling rig when a hydraulic cylinder seized and jammed the drill head. The employee had to manually force the cylinder to release, but the hydraulic hose burst as the pressure finally released, spraying high‑pressure fluid across the platform. No one was injured, but the sudden hose failure exposed workers to a splash of hot oil and the risk of a fire.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was seen walking around the fuel storage tank area without wearing the required safety gloves. He was only wearing a light jacket and had his phone in his pocket, which is against the PPE policy for that zone. The employee was about a foot away from a leaking hose line when his unprotected hand brushed the metal valve, causing a small splash of fuel that splattered onto his sleeve. The incident was quickly contained, but it highlighted a clear lapse in PPE compliance and a potential for a larger spill.

While working the day shift on Rig 4, a contractor slipped on a wet patch near the valve pit because the spill was not contained. The contractor stumbled, nearly falling onto the exposed pipe but managed to catch himself on a nearby scaffold. No one was hurt, but the spill had exposed a trip hazard that could have caused a serious injury if the contractor had not reacted quickly.

During the night shift on Rig 4, a company employee noticed a faint orange glow near the gas line access panel. He pulled the flame arrestor aside to inspect a potential leak, but the panel was missing its safety latch, exposing the valve. The employee quickly sealed the valve and called for a safety review before the gas could ignite, preventing a fire near miss.

While on the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee was walking across the loading bay when a maintenance truck accidentally cut across the pedestrian path. The driver almost ran into the employee, but the employee stepped back in time. The incident highlighted that the barrier posts along the loading area were not in place and the truck's rearview mirrors were obstructed. The employee was unharmed but the event prompted an immediate review of the pedestrian routing and barrier placement.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the maintenance bay when a spill from the coolant system wasn’t cleaned up quickly enough. The worker caught himself before falling, but the slippery surface posed a serious risk for anyone walking through the area. No one was injured, but the incident highlighted that spill containment and timely cleanup are critical to avoid future trips or slips.
An employee was removing a basket from behind a forklift. The forklift ran over his left foot, lacerating the bottom of the foot. The employee was hospitalized.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee entered a storage silo without wearing the required harness. The safety cage that should have been attached to the rigging was missing, so the employee slipped and almost fell onto the bulk material. He stopped the operation immediately, and the incident was reported to the safety officer.

Night shift at Drilling Unit F, a contractor was walking across the wet hatchway when a loose cable slipped out of its holder and rolled onto the floor. He almost slipped, but managed to catch himself on the railing. The cable was still hanging at the end of the workbench, so the cable holder had to be replaced before the crew could resume drilling.

On the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was carrying a bulk container down the maintenance aisle. The floor had a sudden patch of wet oil from a recent leak, and he slipped, nearly falling onto a stack of pallets. The fall was caught by the surrounding crew, and the container was moved to a dry spot before anyone was hurt.

At Pipeline Yard D on the day shift, a contractor was attempting to disconnect a section of the 300 psi line for maintenance. The isolation valve had been left open due to a miscommunication, and when the contractor tried to lift the valve handle, a sudden surge of pressure burst the valve seal, sending a spray of high‑pressure fluid across the work area. The contractor was splashed, and the hydraulic pressure caused a nearby guard rail to buckle, leaving a small gap in the safety barrier that could have let debris fall onto the track. The incident was quickly contained, but the valve failure and missing guard highlight a serious lapse in energy isolation.

During the day shift at Drilling Unit F, a company employee entered a venting shaft that had no temporary gas detection equipment in place. As he was lowering the harness, the ladder he was using slipped on the slick concrete, and he almost fell into the confined space. Luckily, the fall was avoided by a teammate who grabbed his forearm just in time. The incident highlighted the missing safety barrier that should have prevented ladder movement in that area.

While loading crude at Terminal C during the day shift, a contractor was operating a forklift that had a faulty load‑sway sensor. As he backed out of the dock, the sensor failed to trigger the warning and the forklift tipped, throwing the pallet of chemicals onto the floor. The contractor escaped unharmed, but the spill required a quick clean‑up to prevent any fire hazard.
An employee exited a truck, which then rolled over him. The employee sustained injuries to the skull and legs.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a company employee was walking to the loading dock when a service truck entered the pedestrian zone without stopping. The driver swerved to avoid a rock, causing the employee to stumble and almost get hit. Luckily the truck slowed enough to avoid a collision, but the employee had a minor bruise and the incident highlighted that the safety barrier that should have separated vehicles from workers was missing that day.

At Pipeline Yard D during the night shift, a contractor was operating a jackhammer to remove a rusted pipe section. While digging, the contractor hit the steel pipe frame and the jackhammer’s safety guard had snapped off, so the operator’s arm got caught and dragged close to the moving conveyor belt. Luckily, the belt was already stopped and the contractor only bruised his forearm, but the incident shows the guard failure and the risk of machinery contact.

On Rig 4 during the day shift a company employee was inspecting the hydraulic pump when the guardrail on the motor mount fell off, exposing the moving shaft. The employee was only a few feet away but didn't hit the shaft because the automatic shut‑off engaged just in time. The guardrail will need replacement before the next shift.

Late night in Maintenance Shop H, a company employee was turning off the hydraulic press when a latch failed to lock and the arm swung free, nearly striking the worker’s wrist. The employee grabbed the arm just in time and was able to stop the motion before any injury occurred. The latch needs to be inspected and replaced.

On the night shift at Rig 4, a company employee slipped on a wet patch near the spillway because the usual warning tape was missing. The worker almost fell into the drainage trench but caught themselves on a nearby pipe. The slip was quickly cleaned up and tape re‑installed before the shift ended.
A maintenance employee was using a sledge hammer to remove an end cap on an axle to a ride. The sledge hammer struck the employee's right pinky finger, crushing it.
An employee was climbing down a ladder with a tool bag swung over his shoulder when it swung and struck him. He suffered an infection and was hospitalized.

An employee was working from a bucket truck to restore a power line. The boom was lowered and struck a tree, causing the employee to be ejected from the bucket. The employee fell approximately 25 feet to the ground below, resulting in fractures to both femurs and one fractured bone in their back.

While doing a routine inspection at Rig 4 on the day shift, a company employee noticed a faint hiss coming from the gas line near the valve station. He immediately shut down the valve but found the safety isolation block was missing, so the leak could have spread into the work area. The employee marked the spot and called the supervisor to install a proper barrier before the leak could ignite.

During the night shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking across the loading dock when a maintenance truck, just exiting the yard, drove straight into him. The driver was distracted by a phone call and didn't see the pedestrian until the last second. The employee was knocked to the ground, bruised his arm and ankle, and had to be helped back to the break room for treatment.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee entered a vent hood that had not been properly sealed. The air test showed a sudden drop in oxygen levels, but the worker noticed the alarm and backed out before any breathing difficulties occurred. The incident was flagged because the confinement barrier had been omitted, but fortunately no injury happened.

During the day shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee entered a vent pipe that was supposed to be sealed. The lockout tag was missing, so the pipe was still pressurized. He nearly got sucked into the pipe before the supervisor noticed and shut the valve down. The incident was a close call but the employee was fine.
notes: LOTO also implicated; picked confined-space entry as primary hazard

text: An employee was laying glue on the corner of a three-story commercial flat roof to apply new thermoplastic polyolefin roofing material. He lost his balance and fell at least 35 feet to the concrete ground below. The employee sustained fractures.

Night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was walking near the loading dock when a delivery truck entered the pedestrian lane. The driver ran the stop sign and nearly collided with the employee, who stepped back just in time. The incident highlighted the lack of a clear traffic separation barrier in that area.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was walking along the perimeter of the maintenance yard when a delivery truck accelerated to pass the lane and brushed the contractor’s shoulder. The truck’s brakes had just been serviced, but the operator was distracted by a phone call, so he didn’t slow down until it was too late. The contractor didn’t lose his footing, but he was startled and stepped into a nearby storage area, narrowly avoiding a stack of pallets that had not been properly secured.

At Terminal C during the day shift, a company employee was walking near the storage tanks when a faint odor of gas wafted past. The worker stopped immediately, turned off the nearby valve, and called the safety officer. No fire erupted, but the incident highlighted a missing gas leak detector in that area.
A beam struck an ironworker during a demolition. The ironworker suffered skull, neck, and wrist fractures, as well as lacerations to the head and leg.

While shutting down the 30 ft line at Pipeline Yard D during the day shift, a company employee forgot to lock the isolation valve. The valve slipped open when the crew started pumping, sending a burst of pressurized fluid straight into the yard. Fortunately the employee and crew were wearing PPE, but the sudden surge knocked over a stack of crates and splashed oil onto the ground, creating a slick that could have caused a slip. The incident was reported immediately and the valve was reseated and checked.

During the night shift at Loading Bay G, a company employee was moving a pallet up onto the mezzanine platform when the hand rail slipped. He caught himself but lost balance and almost dropped 4 feet to the concrete floor below. The fall was stopped by a nearby safety net that was partially installed, but the employee still slipped and twisted his ankle. The incident was logged as a near‑miss.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a contractor was climbing the ladder to access the top of the rig tower when he slipped on a wet rung. He was able to grab the nearby handhold and avoided falling. The incident was logged as a near-miss, and the ladder was inspected for missing guardrails before work resumed.

On the day shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was inspecting the hydraulic pump when he noticed the isolation valve was still open. He tried to close it, but the valve stuck and didn’t seal, allowing hydraulic fluid to flow into the tank. A small spray of fluid hit the worker’s clothing, causing a mild burn on his forearm. The incident was reported and the valve was replaced before any serious injury occurred.

On or about 6/8/2016, at approximately 1:15, an employee was placing a stencil inside a mold when a piece (known as a cradle) fell down from inside the top of the mold and struck/partially amputated the employee's left middle and ring fingers.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was seen walking across the loading bay without a safety vest or hard hat. He was only a few feet away from the conveyor belt when a loose cable slipped, almost pulling him down. The incident was stopped by a quick stop of the belt, but the lack of PPE still put him at serious risk. The supervisor had to remind everyone that PPE is mandatory before the next shift begins.

Night shift at Rig 4, a contractor was attempting to enter a vent shaft to replace a damaged pipe. He didn’t use the required air‑monitoring device before opening the hatch, and a sudden surge of gas was detected when he stepped inside. The contractor immediately stopped and called for a safe‑air check, but the hatch seal was loose and the door didn’t latch properly, allowing a small leak of hydrocarbon vapor to escape into the confined space. The incident was contained with no injuries, but it highlighted that the safety barrier on the hatch was missing and needed to be repaired before the next entry.

During the night shift at Rig 4, a contractor was operating the drilling rig’s feed‑water pump. While adjusting the pressure valve, the safety guard on the motor housing was found removed for maintenance, and the contractor’s hand slipped onto the rotating shaft. Fortunately, the emergency stop was triggered before contact occurred, but the incident highlights the missing barrier that could have caused serious injury.
An employee stepped out of a moving vehicle, fell, and struck his head. He was hospitalized.
An employee was moving a scaffold when he slipped on some stones and fell off a retaining wall onto his side, breaking ribs.

Night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was walking near the unloading bay when she failed to wear the required safety harness. The ladder she was climbing was unsecured and the guardrail was missing. She slipped slightly but caught herself, and the ladder snapped, dropping a tool that narrowly missed a fellow worker. The incident was logged as a near‑miss and the missing guardrail was immediately fixed.

During the day shift at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor entered a storage tank without the required safety barrier in place. He was working on a routine inspection when he noticed a slight oxygen deficiency and immediately pulled out, but the tank door was still partially open, letting a draft in. The contractor managed to escape without injury, but the missing barrier is a clear violation of our confined space entry procedures.

At Pipeline Yard D on the night shift, a contractor was working on the rooftop of the storage tank when a handrail that was supposed to support him slid off the steel bracket. He nearly fell but caught himself on the edge of the tank, and no one was injured. The handrail was found to be improperly installed and the safety guard was missing. The incident was reported to the safety officer immediately.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a company employee was seen walking through the high‑pressure pipe area without a hard hat or face shield. The worker was carrying a toolbox and didn’t notice the guard rail had been removed for maintenance. A bolt from the pipe brushed the worker’s neck, and the metal splintered, narrowly missing the head. The employee was shaken but not seriously injured, and the incident was logged as a PPE noncompliance near‑miss.

An employee was performing manual labor to build a solar farm outside when he began feeling unwell and experienced severe cramps in his stomach, legs, neck, jaw, and hands. He was hospitalized for dehydration and kidney malfunction due to heat stress.

While walking from the rig house to the drill rig on Rig 4 during the day shift, a company employee slipped on a wet patch left by the de-icing spray that had been used earlier. The employee caught himself on the rig wall just before falling, but the splash had left a small area of slick floor, indicating the de-icing area was not properly cordoned off. No one was injured, but the incident highlighted a potential slip/trip hazard that needs immediate attention.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was working on the flare stack when a sudden gas leak was detected near the piping. The employee noticed a faint odor of methane and immediately shut the valve, but the leak had already produced a small, unburned puff of flame that flashed briefly before going out. No one was injured, but the incident highlighted that the gas detection alarm in that area had been offline for a week, so we flagged it for immediate maintenance.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking on the walk‑way when a maintenance truck drove too close and almost hit him. The employee had to jump out of the way, but the truck’s bumper struck the rail that should have been a safety barrier, showing the barrier was missing or ineffective. The incident was a near‑miss; the employee was only slightly bruised.

During the night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a company employee entered a sealed inspection pit to check a weld joint. While inside, the ventilation fan failed to start, and the worker began feeling dizziness. The employee immediately exited, but the pit had no backup airflow system, so the air quality quickly deteriorated. No injuries occurred, but the incident highlighted that the safety barrier – the automatic fan system – was missing.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee was walking through the loading bay without wearing a high‑visibility vest and a hard hat, even though the area was flagged for PPE requirements. The employee was nearly struck by a forklift that passed close to the loading line, and the lack of protective gear almost resulted in a serious injury. Fortunately, the forklift operator saw the employee and stopped in time, but the incident highlighted a clear PPE noncompliance issue that needs immediate attention.

At Drilling Unit F during the day shift, a contractor was entering a wellhead hatch that had no proper entry lock. He slipped on the wet metal surface and almost fell into the confined space. The hatch was found to be missing its safety barrier, so the contractor had to back out quickly before any serious injury occurred.

At Terminal C on the day shift, a company employee was walking through the loading bay when he failed to wear a safety helmet and eye protection. While checking the tank feed line, he slipped on a wet patch and nearly hit a valve, but the valve was still in the off position, so there was no release of gas. The incident was recorded as a near‑miss because the missing PPE almost caused an eye injury.

On April 13, 2015, at approximately 1:30 p.m., an employee was shot in the left hand. Prior to the incident, a well tender found an issue at a well site. The well tender contacted a roustabout crew to repair and clean the area. The injured employee responded to the job to oversee the work, take pictures, and complete an incident report. After completing his work, he was driving away from the site and was stopped by a suspect dressed in camouflage, standing in the road. The suspect stood on the passenger side of the truck, played a recording that said "stop drilling," and pointed a gun at the employee's head. The employee grabbed the gun and shoved it away from his head; the gun fired into his left hand.  The employee drove off and was hospitalized.
notes: workplace violence/gunshot; not covered by the 8 LSR categories

text: During the night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was entering a drainage pit that had no safety barrier in place. He slipped on a slick spot inside the pit and nearly fell in; fortunately he caught himself on a nearby pipe, but the incident highlighted that the pit entry was not properly secured and the confined space entry protocol was not followed.

During the night shift at Rig 4, a company employee began an entry into a vent shaft without the required air‑monitoring equipment on. While inside, the worker noticed a sudden drop in oxygen levels but didn’t have a backup alarm, so he quickly exited to avoid a potential asphyxiation risk. The incident highlighted that the portable oxygen sensor was left in the truck, and the team is reviewing the checklist to prevent a repeat.

During the day shift at Loading Bay G, a contractor was operating a forklift when it suddenly tipped over onto the loading pallet, spilling a small amount of diesel. The forklift's backup alarm had been disabled, so the driver didn't hear the approach of a nearby loading truck and almost collided with it. The incident was a near‑miss, but the spill caused a slip hazard for the crew.

During the day shift at Storage Site E, a contractor was installing a new storage rack. He skipped his hard hat and safety glasses because he was in a hurry, even though the area was marked as a high‑fall zone. When a hydraulic valve unexpectedly released pressure, a burst pipe sprayed hot coolant over the floor. The contractor’s bare hands were splattered, and the incident was called a near‑miss because he was immediately pulled to a safe spot and the fire suppression system kicked in before any serious burns occurred.

At Storage Site E on the day shift a contractor was attempting to close the isolation valve on a 300 psi gas line when the valve failed to lock and slipped open. The contractor didn’t notice the opening until a small burst of gas sprayed onto the work area, knocking him down. Luckily the gas escaped into a vent, so only a brief, localized pressure spike and a minor burn were reported. The incident was flagged as an energy isolation failure that required an immediate lock‑out procedure.

During the night shift at Storage Site E, a company employee was working on the loading dock when a forklift’s hydraulic cylinder seized, causing the pallet jack to tilt and almost roll into the safety gate. The employee quickly grabbed the pallet jack to stabilize it, but the hydraulic valve failed to engage properly, which left the machinery in an unsafe position for the rest of the shift. Thankfully no one was injured, but the incident highlighted that the hydraulic safety cut‑off was not functioning and the gate was only partially secured.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee was checking a valve when a sudden gas leak alarm sounded. The employee noticed a faint odor of gas and immediately shut off the valve, but the smell spread across the bay. He had to pull back before the pressure built up, so no fire broke out, but the safety barrier on the valve had been removed for maintenance and wasn’t replaced in time.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a contractor was attempting to enter a storage tank for a routine inspection. He forgot to secure the confined space entry gate, and the hatch slipped open as he approached, nearly letting him fall into the tank. The incident was a near-miss because he managed to grab the railing in time and was stopped by the safety supervisor. The gate was later replaced with a proper lockable barrier to prevent a repeat.

Night shift at Terminal C: a contractor was operating the loading crane when the boom slipped off the designated track and hit the nearby storage tank. The crane’s safety bar was missing, so the load tipped over and spilled a small amount of fuel onto the floor, creating a fire risk that was quickly extinguished by the crew. The contractor was shaken but unharmed; we inspected the crane and installed a new safety bar before the next shift.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a company employee entered a venting hood that had not been properly sealed for the scheduled maintenance. While inside, the worker noticed a sudden rush of cool air and a faint hiss from the exhaust line; the confined space seal was missing, allowing air to escape and reducing oxygen levels. The employee quickly exited the space, but the incident revealed that the safety barrier was not in place and the confined space entry procedures were not followed, creating a serious hazard.

Night shift at Drilling Unit F, a contractor was going in for a routine inspection of the gas‑tight vent stack. He slipped on the wet concrete and fell into the vent’s access hatch before he could secure the hatch. The hatch was open because the lock‑out tag was missing, so he ended up in the confined space and had to be pulled out by the crew.

During disassembly of a spent perforating-gun tool string, an employee attempted to carry the setting tool (designed to set a plug in the well) section from the external stands into the trailer for breakdown. When he lifted the setting tool in the vertical position, he placed his right hand over and into the open end of the sleeve. At that point, the internal mandrel shifted further up to the open end. His right middle fingertip was pinched by the mandrel and the set-screw opening at the end of the sleeve, amputating the distal phalanx.

During the night shift at Refinery B, I was performing a routine inspection in the vent stack. While entering the confined space, the hatch latch jammed and I couldn’t close it securely. I had to pull it back out to keep my breathing mask on, so the space was open for a few minutes and the ventilation fan cycled on and off. It was a close call – a quick exit would have let me lose my mask and inhale the stack gases.

During the day shift at Rig 4, a company employee was entering a maintenance hatch that had no proper lockout/tagout on place. While going in, the ventilation fan suddenly failed and the air inside the hatch went stale, so the worker had to hold his breath and pull back quickly, almost getting caught on the hatch door. The incident was a near miss because the hatch latch was not properly engaged, but the employee was unharmed.

On Rig 4 during the night shift a contractor was tightening a valve when a small flame sparked from a loose pipe fitting. The fire was quickly doused by the contractor’s own fire extinguisher, but the incident highlighted a missing fire barrier that should have contained the spark. No one was hurt, and the crew shut the valve off and called for a safety inspection before continuing work.
An employee was manually lifting a roll of fabric material with a metal pole. The employee placed the pole into its holder and pinched their left index finger resulting in a partial amputation.

In Pipeline Yard D during the day shift, a company employee slipped on a patch of oil that had leaked from a cracked pipe. He didn’t fall, but he lost his footing and almost tripped over a loose, unmarked pipe section that was blocking the access route. The spill was quickly mopped up and the damaged pipe was replaced before any further slips could happen.

During the night shift at Terminal C, a contractor was working on the maintenance of the LPG line. While attempting to isolate the line, the valve failed to lock into the off position, leaving the line still energized. The contractor had to quickly pull away and warn the crew, but a few meters downstream the pressure relief valve tripped, sending a burst of gas into the work area. Fortunately, no one was injured, but the incident shows the isolation procedure was not properly followed and the safety barrier was ineffective.

At Rig 4 on the night shift, a company employee noticed a faint burning smell coming from the tank area. While inspecting the gas lines, the worker saw a small flame flare up near a damaged pipe, but the automatic fire suppression system kicked in before anything spread, so no fire actually broke out. The incident was a near miss, but it highlighted that the protective barrier around the pipe had been missing a seal and needed immediate repair.
notes: fire event but no explicit hot-work task; borderline

text: At Rig 4 on the day shift, a company employee entered a small vent shaft to replace a faulty valve. While inside, he realized the breathing apparatus was not properly sealed, so he had to exit immediately to avoid inhaling toxic fumes. The entry platform’s guard rail had been removed for maintenance, but the employee stopped short of the edge and used his hands to keep himself from falling. No injuries, but the incident shows the need to keep safety barriers in place during confined space work.
notes: work-at-height also implicated via missing guard rail; picked confined-space entry as primary

text: During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking across the yard when a maintenance truck drove through the pedestrian crossing zone. The driver didn’t see the employee and swerved, nearly scraping her shin and causing her to stumble. Fortunately, the employee only suffered a minor bruise and there was no injury.

During the day shift on Rig 4 a contractor was working on the access ladder when he ignored the mandatory helmet requirement and walked around without a hard hat. He nearly fell off the ladder when a loose bolt on the handrail slipped, but the fall was averted because the guardrail was still in place. The incident was logged as a near-miss.

An employee and a co-worker were working to pack up pallets on pallet banding equipment. The co-worker was holding the strap as the employee was utilizing a clamp. The employee's right thumb was caught in a pinch point on the clamp, resulting in amputation.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee was walking near the storage tank area when they noticed a faint hiss of gas. They immediately shut off the valve, but the safety barrier was partially missing, so a small burst of vapor drifted towards the exit corridor, making it a close call. The employee reported the incident, and the gas was vented safely, but the barrier issue was logged for repair.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a contractor was checking the vent system on the eastern flue stack when a small gas leak was detected by the handheld detector. The contractor immediately shut off the valve, but the burst pipe had already released a cloud of flammable gas that drifted into the adjacent storage area. Thankfully, no ignition source was present and the leak was contained before it could ignite, but the incident highlighted a missing safety barrier around the vent line.

During the day shift on Rig 4 a contractor was operating a portable drilling rig when the safety guard on the drill bit fell off; the contractor didn’t notice and the bit slipped, scraping the floor and creating a large splintered steel spill that almost got stepped on by a nearby crew member. The contractor stopped the rig immediately and called for a safety check, but the guard was not reinstalled until the end of the shift.

At Drilling Unit F, during the night shift, a contractor was operating the hydraulic jack to lift a drill string section when the locking pin failed to engage. The jack slipped, dropping the weight onto the adjacent pipe ladder and shattering it. The contractor escaped with a minor bruised arm, but the incident highlighted a missing safety guard on the jack’s pivot.

While working the day shift at Drilling Unit F, a contractor tripped over a loose cable that had come out of the maintenance belt. The cable was lying across the walk‑way and the contractor slipped, but only bruised his knee and had to step out for a quick check. The area had no safety barrier or warning flag, so the risk of a serious fall was high.

Night shift at Terminal C, a contractor was performing routine maintenance on a storage tank. He had left the isolation valves open, thinking they were already closed from a previous check. While moving the valve handle, the contractor got a sudden jolt and a burst of steam hit him, scalding his forearm. The valve lockout tag was missing, so the energy isolation failed and caused the minor burn.

During the day shift on Rig 4, a contractor was using the hydraulic lift to reposition a drill string when the lift’s emergency stop lever failed to engage. The hydraulic pump continued to operate, and the lift began to move upward unexpectedly, narrowly missing a nearby support beam. The contractor stopped immediately and reported the incident to the shift supervisor.

During the day shift at Refinery B a contractor was attempting to enter a maintenance hatch for a cooling pipe. He started the entry but noticed that the ventilation fan was off, so he stopped and called for a technician to start it. The contractor’s safety harness was already attached, but the backstop bar that normally blocks the hatch was missing, so he had to improvise with a rope. Once the fan was started he was able to complete the inspection without incident.
notes: worker stopped before real exposure; borderline on severity/sif

text: During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee climbed into a storage tank to perform routine inspection. The entry hatch seal had been left loose, and when the employee opened the hatch, a small pocket of low-oxygen air was released, causing him to feel light‑headed. He quickly backed out, and the safety team checked the hatch before allowing anyone else to enter.
An employee was running an edger. While pushing a log through the edger, the log kicked back, striking the employee in the stomach. The employee sustained a cut to his stomach.

Night shift at Pipeline Yard D, a contractor was moving a 30‑inch pipe segment without his hard hat and steel‑toed boots. He stepped onto a small pile‑up of gravel, and a heavy clamp slipped off the pipe, striking his left leg. The impact ripped through the leather of his knee pad, but no serious injury was reported because he was wearing a full‑sleeve shirt. The incident highlighted a clear failure in PPE compliance.

During the day shift at Terminal C, a company employee tried to enter the storage tank through the hatch while the valve was still open. He noticed a faint smell of hydrocarbons but stopped and called for a check. The hatch lock was not engaged, so the employee was almost sucked into the tank before a colleague intervened.

At the Pipeline Yard D during the day shift, a contractor was walking down the access lane without his hard hat or high‑visibility vest. When he passed the gas line inspection point, a loose pipe cap fell and landed on the ground. The contractor quickly ducked to avoid injury, but the lack of PPE meant he could not see the falling debris and almost got hit. The incident was logged as a near miss.

At Drilling Unit F on the day shift, a contractor was lowering a tool ladder from the platform when the guard rail at the top edge failed to hold. The ladder slipped, and the contractor nearly fell into the wellhead area; the fall was stopped by a nearby safety net but the contractor landed on his knee and had a minor sprain. The guard rail was found to be loose and had to be reinstalled before work could resume.

During the day shift at Refinery B, a company employee entered a vent stack for maintenance but the access hatch was stuck and did not seal properly. While inside, the hatch slid off, dropping the worker about two feet onto the steel floor, but he was able to recover quickly and report the incident. The missing latch on the hatch created an immediate confined space hazard that could have trapped him if the hatch had fully collapsed.
